text: Lessons 7 and 8 assumed you already know which dataset you're labeling. In practice, most organizations have far more sensitive data scattered across their systems than anyone has fully inventoried. This lesson covers how to find it before someone else does.

Sensitive data hides in predictable places: an old CSV export from a retired system, a spreadsheet someone built for a one-off analysis and never deleted, a backup sitting in a forgotten storage bucket, or a log file that was only ever meant to record errors but accidentally captured a Social Security number swept up in a raw request payload. None of it was ever classified, because nobody knew it was there.

Real discovery tooling combines three techniques. Pattern and regex-based scanning checks whether content matches the shape of sensitive data, a nine-digit SSN pattern, a credit-card checksum, regardless of what the column is named. Keyword and metadata-based discovery looks at the names of things, column names like ssn or credit_card, fast but it misses sensitive data in a generically named column. Sampling-based scanning pulls a representative sample of rows and statistically estimates how much of the whole dataset looks sensitive, instead of checking every row.

This capability isn't hypothetical. Microsoft Purview includes sensitive information type detection. AWS Macie is Amazon's purpose-built service for discovering sensitive data in S3. Google Cloud DLP offers similar inspection within Google Cloud. These are named here because they're real and worth knowing exist, not as a feature walkthrough.

Discovery is a precondition for classification, not an add-on. A perfectly designed scheme only applied to datasets someone happened to remember still leaves every undiscovered file completely unprotected. Next up: actually applying classification labels to what you've found.
